topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Control access to a service while preserving the operation callers already know. Worked example: A lazy cached opening-hour service. One proxy keeps permission, lazy ownership, and cache state beside the service access they control. optional distinguishes no result from a valid zero result.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Use a substitute with the same service interface.
Trace lazy construction, cache hits, and invalidation.
Keep permission checks ahead of cached results.

blocks.text: Subject declares a common service interface. RealSubject performs the underlying work. Proxy implements that interface and decides whether to delegate, reject, reuse a result, or prepare the real service first. Client code can call either through Subject. The common C++ signature permits substitution, but the behavioral contract must also describe failures, freshness, and any other visible change.

cards.question: What problem does Proxy address?
cards.answer: Control access to a service while preserving the operation callers already know. Worked example: A lazy cached opening-hour service. One proxy keeps permission, lazy ownership, and cache state beside the service access they control. optional distinguishes no result from a valid zero result.

cards.question: What is Proxy?
cards.answer: A substitute service object that controls access, location, or lifecycle while keeping the service interface.

cards.question: What is Lazy initialization?
cards.answer: Creating an object only when it is first needed.

cards.question: What is Cache hit?
cards.answer: A request answered from an already stored result.

cards.question: What is Cache invalidation?
cards.answer: Declaring a remembered result unusable so a later request must fetch again.

cards.question: What is Stale data?
cards.answer: Remembered data that is no longer known to match the current source.

cards.question: Why must the access check happen before returning cached_?
cards.answer: Permission may have been revoked since the cache was filled. Returning the cached value first would bypass the new policy.

cards.question: Does the attached Proxy lazily create its RealSubject when Request is first called?
cards.answer: No. It creates an owned copy in its constructor. Our HoursProxy adds lazy creation explicitly and tests that no service exists before first permitted use.

cards.question: Why must permission be checked before consulting a populated cache?
cards.answer: A cached value is still protected information. Returning it first would let a client read after access was revoked.

cards.question: What is the difference between unloaded and uncached here?
cards.answer: Unloaded means no RealHours object exists. Uncached means no remembered opening value exists. Invalidation can clear the value while retaining the already constructed service.

cards.question: Why use optional<int> instead of zero as the empty-cache marker?
cards.answer: Midnight is a valid zero opening hour. optional represents absence separately from all valid integer values.

cards.question: Does caching promise that opening always returns current source data?
cards.answer: No. This proxy explicitly allows staleness until invalidate or refresh. Freshness is part of the contract and must be clear to callers.

cards.question: When would direct access be simpler than this proxy?
cards.answer: When source reads are cheap and no caching, delayed construction or access control is needed. An extra proxy then adds state without solving a real problem.

cards.question: Why does a denied refresh leave the old cache intact?
cards.answer: Permission is tested before invalidation. A rejected request must not change the cache or perform a source read under this contract.

cards.question: What lifetime issue is not solved by owning RealHours?
cards.answer: Both the proxy and real service borrow Source. Owning the service does not extend the source's lifetime; the caller must keep Source alive.

topics.title: A cheap question can trigger expensive work
topics.summary: A visitor display asks for a building's opening hour. In a real system that answer may require opening a connection or reading a remote schedule. This example uses a tiny in-memory Source so the behavior is deterministic. The source hour starts at eight, and a reads counter records real-service requests. The interface accepts hours already supplied by a trusted source; it does not validate a full calendar or time zone.

blocks.text: The simplest caller invokes the real service every time. That is appropriate when the service is cheap and fresh data matters more than reuse. The new requirements are to avoid creating the real service until needed, reuse the most recently fetched hour until told it is stale, and deny reads when local permission has been revoked. Repeating those rules at every caller would spread state management and make it easy to return a cached value after access was removed.

discussion.question: If a source changes from eight to nine, must an already cached answer immediately become nine?
discussion.answer: Not under this example's contract. The cache may return eight until explicit invalidation. Freshness and access permission are separate rules that the design must state clearly.

topics.title: Use the same interface with an access-controlling substitute
topics.summary: A proxy is a substitute object that controls access to another service while offering the same interface. Hours defines opening(). RealHours reads Source and increments its reads counter. HoursProxy also implements opening, but it checks permission, checks its cache, creates RealHours if necessary, and calls it only when a fresh value is needed. Code written against Hours can use either object.

blocks.text: The proxy holds a Source reference and an optional unique_ptr<RealHours>. The pointer starts empty. Constructing the proxy therefore does not construct RealHours. Creating the real object only on first demand is called lazy initialization. Once created, the real service remains owned by the proxy even if cached data is invalidated. The two states answer different questions: is a service object present, and is there a remembered result?

Caching means retaining a result for later reuse. std::optional<int> stores either no value or one integer. It is a better representation than using zero as an empty marker because midnight, hour zero, is valid. Testing cached_ asks whether a value exists; it does not ask whether the stored integer is nonzero. Dereferencing it with *cached_ reads that value only after the program knows it is present.

topics.title: Permission comes before the fast path
topics.summary: opening first checks allowed_. If false, it throws runtime_error immediately. It does this before consulting cached_. Revoking permission must stop both real-service reads and returns of data fetched earlier. A misplaced permission check after the cache hit would deny new reads but still expose old cached data. That is a precise ordering bug, not a reason to abandon caching.

blocks.text: This Boolean permission is a local teaching model, not an authentication system. There is no user identity, secret, network enforcement, or protection against a caller directly using RealHours. In a real application, access decisions need an authoritative policy and a boundary that unauthorized callers cannot bypass. The pattern explains where a check can sit; it does not make the check trustworthy by itself.

After permission succeeds, an engaged cache returns immediately without creating or reading a real service. On a cache miss, the proxy creates RealHours only if real_ is still empty. Then it calls real_->opening, stores the returned integer in cached_, and returns it. The virtual interface is the same, but allowed caching deliberately changes freshness. That semantic difference must be part of the service contract a caller accepts.

topics.title: Trace old data and explicit invalidation
topics.summary: The first opening call sees no cache and no real service. It creates RealHours, reads eight, stores eight, and leaves source.reads equal to one. main changes source.hour to nine. The next opening call still returns eight, and the read counter stays one. That stale value is expected under this cache policy. Stale means no longer known to match the current source.

blocks.text: invalidate calls cached_.reset(), which removes the stored result but leaves real_ alive. The next permitted opening call reuses the already-created service object, reads nine, stores it, and advances reads to two. main then denies access and confirms that even this warm cache cannot be read. After re-enabling access, it changes the source to zero, invalidates, and calls twice. Both calls return zero, but only the first reads the source, leaving the final counter at three.

An invalidation policy says when remembered data stops being usable. This program makes that decision explicit in main. It does not watch Source automatically. A production design might attach a revision number, receive a change notification, use a maximum age, or always fetch fresh data for critical operations. Each choice has a cost and a freshness promise. A cache without a stated invalidation policy is an unfinished design.

topics.title: Object lifetime and failure state
topics.summary: main creates Source before HoursProxy, so the borrowed source outlives the proxy. The proxy owns its RealHours through unique_ptr. RealHours itself borrows the same Source. Destroying the proxy destroys the optional cache and the real-service owner, but it does not destroy Source. Local declaration order supplies the required lifetime arrangement without manual deletion.

blocks.text: At compilation, override checks that both classes implement Hours::opening. The method is not const because obtaining an answer may change the cache and the source's diagnostic counter. A logically read-only business operation can still mutate implementation state; the interface should state that honestly rather than adding mutable everywhere without discussing consequences.

If allocation of RealHours fails, the owner remains empty and the cache remains empty. If a future real-service call throws before returning an integer, assignment to cached_ is not reached, so a miss remains uncached. The example's real service does not throw, but placing assignment after a successful call naturally avoids remembering a fabricated success. The exact state of a real service after its own failure would still depend on that service's contract.

The program is single-threaded. Concurrent calls could race while creating real_, reading Source, or changing cached_. shared ownership or virtual functions would not fix those races. A concurrent version would need synchronization and a clear rule for the order of revocation, invalidation, and in-flight requests. We do not add those mechanisms without the requirement because they would obscure the state transitions being taught.

Hours defaults construction but explicitly deletes copy and move operations. The = delete declarations make service objects stable in place; callers transfer an owning unique_ptr handle when ownership must change. Without this rule, an implicit proxy move would transfer real_ while leaving copied scalar cache and permission state in the source, creating two surprising service identities. Preventing object moves keeps the lifecycle contract simpler. Static type-trait checks verify that HoursProxy is neither copy-constructible nor move-constructible.

topics.title: Distinguish the purpose of similar wrappers
topics.summary: Proxy and Decorator can both implement an interface and contain another implementation. A decorator normally adds independently selectable behavior to a component. A proxy stands in for a service to control access, location, or lifecycle. Our proxy creates its own real service on demand and manages a freshness policy. A diagram alone cannot settle which intent best describes a design; the requirements explain it.

blocks.text: For an inexpensive local value, directly reading Source may be simpler than either wrapper. For a service used exactly once, caching may add memory and complexity without avoiding work. Measure actual request patterns before optimizing. When a proxy is useful, expose enough diagnostics to test the behavior. The reads counter and loaded query let the example verify avoided work rather than merely checking that the printed hour looks right.

topics.title: Worked example: contracts and alternatives
topics.summary: A lazy cached opening-hour service

blocks.title: Requirements
items: Do not create RealHours until the first permitted cache miss.
Reuse cached values until explicit invalidation.
Deny both cached and uncached reads when permission is false.
Treat hour zero as a real cached value.

blocks.text: One proxy keeps permission, lazy ownership, and cache state beside the service access they control. optional distinguishes no result from a valid zero result.

blocks.title: Invariants
items: Denied reads never reach the service or return cached data.
An engaged cache contains a successful prior result.
Invalidation removes the result but does not destroy the service.
Source outlives the proxy and its real service.

blocks.text: Alternative: Direct service calls are simpler when freshness is always required or calls are cheap. A standalone caching function may fit one caller; a proxy fits interchangeable Hours users.

Verification: Checks verify initial unloaded state, first-read construction, reuse without extra reads, stale behavior, explicit refresh after invalidation, denial with a warm cache, and cached zero. They do not test network access, real authentication, or concurrent execution. Compile-time type traits also verify that HoursProxy object copying and moving are disabled.
Maintenance: A useful proxy must document freshness, access checks, and failure behavior as carefully as its interface. Test the work it avoids and the states it preserves.

topics.title: Exercise 12.4: Choose a design
topics.summary: A safety display requires the current source value on every request and the service is cheap. Should it use this cache policy?

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: Freshness is part of correctness.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: No. Use direct service calls or a proxy that checks permission but always fetches. Reusing an old value violates that display requirement, even if it improves speed. A maximum-age policy is appropriate only if the requirement permits that amount of staleness.

topics.summary: Add a test that denial before the first call leaves loaded() false and reads zero. Then allow and call again. State all expected observations.

blocks.title: Explained answer

topics.title: Exercise 12.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: Explain to a teammate why invalidate does not destroy RealHours. Give a case where closing the real service as well could be reasonable.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: A stale result and an unusable connection are different conditions.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: The cached hour may be old while the service object is still useful for another read. Keeping it avoids reconstructing the connection. If a failed or revoked session makes the real service unusable, an explicit reset operation may clear both owner and cache, with separate tests for reconnection.

blocks.title: Solution reasoning
blocks.text: The solution checks permission before invalidating, then calls opening to reuse the ordinary lazy-fetch path. Checking only inside opening after invalidation would erase valid cached state on a denied request, violating the lab requirement. Repeated permission checking is small and keeps the existing opening contract unchanged; a factored private permission helper is a reasonable cleanup.

workshop.title: A lazy cached opening-hour service
workshop.problem: A lazy cached opening-hour service. Do not create RealHours until the first permitted cache miss. Reuse cached values until explicit invalidation. Deny both cached and uncached reads when permission is false. Treat hour zero as a real cached value.
workshop.output:
cached=8
fresh=9
midnight=0
reads=3
cached access denied after revocation

steps.why: The first permitted miss creates and calls RealHours.
A hit follows the explicit cache policy.
The next miss fetches fresh source data.
The warm cache does not bypass access control.
An engaged optional can hold zero without another fetch.

workshop.pitfall: Use if (*cached_) to decide whether the cache contains data. Dereferencing an empty optional is invalid; zero is also incorrectly treated as a miss. Value presence and numeric truth are different questions.

discussion.question: A safety display requires the current source value on every request and the service is cheap. Should it use this cache policy?
discussion.answer: No. Use direct service calls or a proxy that checks permission but always fetches. Reusing an old value violates that display requirement, even if it improves speed. A maximum-age policy is appropriate only if the requirement permits that amount of staleness.

workshop.alternative: Direct service calls are simpler when freshness is always required or calls are cheap. A standalone caching function may fit one caller; a proxy fits interchangeable Hours users.
workshop.design: One proxy keeps permission, lazy ownership, and cache state beside the service access they control. optional distinguishes no result from a valid zero result.
invariants: Denied reads never reach the service or return cached data.
An engaged cache contains a successful prior result.
Invalidation removes the result but does not destroy the service.
Source outlives the proxy and its real service.
workshop.maintenance: A useful proxy must document freshness, access checks, and failure behavior as carefully as its interface. Test the work it avoids and the states it preserves.
workshop.verification: Checks verify initial unloaded state, first-read construction, reuse without extra reads, stale behavior, explicit refresh after invalidation, denial with a warm cache, and cached zero. They do not test network access, real authentication, or concurrent execution. Compile-time type traits also verify that HoursProxy object copying and moving are disabled.
